title: Diluvium. Deucalion et Pyrrha
titleEn: The Flood; Deucalion and Pyrrha — Metamorphoses I.253–415
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Jupiter has judged mankind and found it past saving. He puts his thunderbolts back rather than risk setting the sky itself alight, and drowns the world instead: the south wind is loosed, Neptune gives the rivers their head, and the earth is struck open to let the sea up through it. Ovid's flood is a catalogue of the world inverted — a man rowing where he had ploughed, a fish taken in a treetop, seals lying where goats grazed, dolphins in the woods — and then, when the water falls, of a world handed back empty. Two people are left on Parnassus: Deucalion, son of Prometheus, and Pyrrha, his wife and his cousin. They pray at the moss-grown shrine of Themis and are told to throw the bones of their great mother behind their backs; Pyrrha refuses in horror, Deucalion reads the riddle, and the stones they throw soften into people. The part closes on the reason the whole episode has been building towards: we are a hard race because we came out of stone.

sentences.t: Iamque erat in totas sparsurus fulmina terras:
sentences.l: And now he was about to scatter thunderbolts over all the lands:
sentences.n: 'sparsurus ... erat' is the future participle with 'esse' — 'was on the point of'. The line picks up straight from Lycaon: Jupiter has already resolved on destroying mankind, and the bolt is in his hand.

sentences.t:
sed timuit, ne forte sacer tot ab ignibus aether
conciperet flammas longusque ardesceret axis:
sentences.l:
but he feared, lest by chance the sacred upper air from so many fires
might catch flame and the long axle blaze.
sentences.i: but he took fright: the holy upper air might catch fire from so many bolts at once, and the long axle of the world go up in flame.
sentences.n: 'ne ... conciperet ... ardesceret' is a fear clause — 'ne' with the subjunctive after a verb of fearing, and it means 'lest it should happen', not 'that it should not'. 'axis' is the axle the heavens turn on, so 'longus' says it runs the whole length of the universe.

sentences.t:
esse quoque in fatis reminiscitur, adfore tempus,
quo mare, quo tellus correptaque regia caeli
ardeat et mundi moles obsessa laboret.
sentences.l:
he recalls too that it stands among the fates that a time will come,
in which the sea, in which the land and the palace of heaven, caught up,
shall blaze, and the beleaguered mass of the world be in travail.
sentences.i: he remembers, too, that the fates hold this as well: a time will come when sea and land and the palace of heaven itself shall be caught up and burn, and the beleaguered fabric of the world labour in its agony.
sentences.n: 'esse in fatis' — 'to be among the fates', that is, to stand decreed; 'adfore' is the future infinitive of 'adsum'. The lines look forward to the world's ending by fire, which Ovid stages in Book II when Phaethon loses the sun's chariot.

sentences.t:
Tela reponuntur manibus fabricata Cyclopum:
poena placet diversa, genus mortale sub undis
perdere et ex omni nimbos demittere caelo.
sentences.l:
The weapons are laid back, forged by the hands of the Cyclopes:
a different punishment pleases — to destroy the mortal race
beneath the waves, and to send down rain-clouds out of the whole sky.
sentences.i: The weapons the Cyclopes' hands had forged go back into store: another punishment finds favour — to drown the mortal race beneath the waves, and send the rain down out of every quarter of the sky.
sentences.n: 'poena ... diversa' is the nominative subject of 'placet' — 'a different punishment is pleasing' — and the two infinitives stand in apposition to it, saying what that punishment is. The Cyclopes forge Jupiter's bolts under Etna, so 'tela reponuntur' means the thunderbolts are put away unused.

sentences.t:
Protinus Aeoliis Aquilonem claudit in antris
et quaecumque fugant inductas flamina nubes
emittitque Notum.
sentences.l:
Straightway he shuts Aquilo up in the Aeolian caves,
and whatever blasts drive off the clouds drawn over the sky,
and he sends Notus out.
sentences.i: At once he shuts the North Wind away in the Aeolian caves, and every blast that clears off the clouds once they are drawn over the sky — and lets the South Wind out.
sentences.n: Aquilo is the north wind, dry and clearing; Notus is the south wind, wet. Aeolus keeps the winds penned in his caves. 'inductas' has the clouds 'drawn over' the sky like a covering, which is exactly what these winds undo.

sentences.t:
Madidis Notus evolat alis,
terribilem picea tectus caligine vultum:
sentences.l:
On dripping wings Notus flies out,
veiled as to his terrible face with pitch-black murk:
sentences.i: Out flies the South Wind on dripping wings, his terrible face veiled in pitch-black murk:
sentences.n: 'tectus ... vultum' is a Greek accusative of respect: he is covered *as to* his face. Latin borrows the turn from Greek and Ovid uses it constantly with participles of veiling, dressing and covering — you will meet it again five lines below, with Iris.

sentences.t:
barba gravis nimbis, canis fluit unda capillis;
fronte sedent nebulae, rorant pennaeque sinusque.
sentences.l:
his beard heavy with rain-clouds, water runs from his hoary hair;
on his brow sit mists, his wings drip and his robe-folds drip.
sentences.i: his beard weighed down with rain, water streaming from his grey hair; mists sit on his forehead, and wings and robe alike run wet.
sentences.n: 'barba gravis nimbis' has no verb at all — the Latin sets the picture down and English has to supply 'is'; the three clauses that follow each carry their own verb. 'pennaeque sinusque' is the double '-que ... -que', an epic mannerism for 'both ... and'.

sentences.t:
Utque manu late pendentia nubila pressit,
fit fragor: hinc densi funduntur ab aethere nimbi.
sentences.l:
And when with his hand he pressed the clouds hanging far and wide,
a crash comes: from there dense rain-clouds are poured out of the upper air.
sentences.i: And when his hand squeezed the clouds that hung far and wide, there came a crash: from that moment the dense rain poured down out of the sky.
sentences.n: 'fit fragor' — 'a crash happens'. The storm runs in the present ('evolat', 'fluit', 'sedent', 'rorant', 'funduntur'), with the perfect 'pressit' dropped in for the one completed act; Ovid alternates the two all through to hurry the narrative and to slow it.

sentences.t:
Nuntia Iunonis varios induta colores
concipit Iris aquas alimentaque nubibus adfert.
sentences.l:
Juno's messenger, clothed as to her varied colours,
Iris, draws up waters and brings nourishment to the clouds.
sentences.i: Juno's messenger, dressed in her many colours — Iris — draws the waters up and carries the clouds their food.
sentences.n: 'induta colores' is the accusative of respect again, 'clothed as to her colours'. Iris is the rainbow and Juno's messenger; the ancient account of a rainbow had it drawing seawater up to refill the clouds, and 'alimenta' takes that literally.

sentences.t:
Sternuntur segetes et deplorata coloni
vota iacent, longique perit labor inritus anni.
sentences.l:
The crops are laid flat, and the farmer's prayers lie
lamented, and the fruitless labour of a long year perishes.
sentences.i: The standing corn is beaten flat; the farmer's prayers lie in ruins and wept over, and a long year's labour is lost for nothing.
sentences.n: 'vota' are what he prayed for, here the harvest itself. 'deplorata' is split from 'vota' across the line-end, a hyperbaton Ovid uses to hold a word back; 'inritus' means made void, come to nothing.

sentences.t:
Nec caelo contenta suo est Iovis ira, sed illum
caeruleus frater iuvat auxiliaribus undis.
sentences.l:
Nor is Jove's anger content with its own sky, but his
sea-blue brother helps him with auxiliary waves.
sentences.i: Jove's anger is not content with his own sky: his sea-blue brother comes to his help with reinforcements of water.
sentences.n: The 'caeruleus frater' is Neptune, named by kinship and colour rather than by name — Ovid does this with gods constantly. 'auxiliaribus' is a military word: auxiliary troops sent to a hard-pressed commander.

sentences.t:
Convocat hic amnes. Qui postquam tecta tyranni
intravere sui, “non est hortamine longo
nunc” ait “utendum.
sentences.l:
He calls the rivers together. And when the halls of their own
overlord they had entered, 'long urging is not
now,' he says, 'to be used.
sentences.i: He calls the rivers together; and when they had come into their overlord's halls: 'No long exhortation need be used now,' he says.
sentences.n: 'intravere' is 'intraverunt' — the poetic third-person plural perfect in '-ere', which Ovid reaches for whenever the metre wants it. You will meet it many times in this part. 'Qui' opening the sentence is the connecting relative, 'and they'; and 'non est utendum hortamine' is a gerundive of obligation, with 'utor' taking the ablative.

sentences.t:
Vires effundite vestras:
sic opus est! aperite domos ac mole remota
fluminibus vestris totas inmittite habenas!”
sentences.l:
Pour out your strength:
so there is need! Open your houses, and with the barrier removed
give your rivers the whole of the reins!'
sentences.i: Pour out all your strength — that is what is wanted! Open your gates, take away the dams, and give your rivers their head!'
sentences.n: 'mole remota' is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with X done' phrase where English wants a clause. 'totas inmittite habenas' is the language of chariot-driving: slacken the reins altogether and let the team run.

sentences.t:
Iusserat; hi redeunt ac fontibus ora relaxant
et defrenato volvuntur in aequora cursu.
sentences.l:
He had commanded; these go back and slacken the mouths at their springs
and are rolled down into the plains in unbridled course.
sentences.i: The order given, back they go, loose the mouths of their springs, and roll down to the open levels with the bit out of their teeth.
sentences.n: Pluperfect 'Iusserat', then straight into the present 'redeunt': the perfect closes the command, the present makes the flood happen now. 'defrenato cursu' keeps the reins of the previous line going — un-bridled.

sentences.t:
Ipse tridente suo terram percussit: at illa
intremuit motuque vias patefecit aquarum.
sentences.l:
He himself struck the earth with his trident: and she
trembled, and by the movement laid open ways for the waters.
sentences.i: Neptune himself struck the earth with his trident: and she shuddered, and the shock opened roads for the water.
sentences.n: 'illa' is the earth, feminine, and 'intremuit' treats her as a living body that shivers — Ovid keeps her animate right through 'patefecit'. 'motu' is an ablative of means, by the shock of the blow.

sentences.t:
Exspatiata ruunt per apertos flumina campos
cumque satis arbusta simul pecudesque virosque
tectaque cumque suis rapiunt penetralia sacris.
sentences.l:
Spread beyond their bounds the rivers rush through open fields,
and together with the crops the orchards, and at once flocks and men
and houses, and with their own sacred things they sweep away the inmost shrines.
sentences.i: The rivers, out of their channels, rush across the open country and carry off the orchards along with the crops, flocks and men together, and houses, and the inner shrines with the holy things still standing in them.
sentences.n: 'exspatiata' is 'having gone out of its own space', said of a river leaving its bed. The piled '-que ... -que ... -que' shoves the losses together without a pause. 'penetralia' is the innermost room of a house, where the household gods stood; 'cum suis sacris' means they go under with their gods still in place.

sentences.t:
Siqua domus mansit potuitque resistere tanto
indeiecta malo, culmen tamen altior huius
unda tegit, pressaeque latent sub gurgite turres.
sentences.l:
If any house remained, and, un-cast-down, was able to stand against
so great a calamity, still a higher wave covers
its roof-ridge, and towers, pressed under, lie hidden beneath the flood.
sentences.i: If any house stood, and held out unshaken against so great a ruin, still a higher wave came over its ridge-pole, and the towers went under and lay hidden in the flood.
sentences.n: 'altior' is a comparative with nothing named to measure against — higher than the house itself. It is also split from its noun across the line-break, 'altior' closing 289 and 'unda' opening 290, so the reader has the height a whole line before he has the wave.

sentences.t:
Iamque mare et tellus nullum discrimen habebant:
omnia pontus erant; deerant quoque litora ponto.
sentences.l:
And now sea and land had no distinction between them:
all was sea; and the sea had no shores either.
sentences.n: 'omnia pontus erant' — a neuter plural subject, a singular predicate noun, and a plural verb: 'all things were sea'. 'quoque' here is the plain adverb 'too'; watch the word, because elsewhere the same letters are 'quo-que', 'and with which'. 'deerant' is scanned as two syllables, its vowels run together, which is why some editions print 'derant'.

sentences.t:
Occupat hic collem, cumba sedet alter adunca
et ducit remos illic, ubi nuper ararat,
sentences.l:
This man seizes a hill; another sits in a curved skiff
and plies the oars there, where lately he had ploughed;
sentences.i: One man takes to a hilltop; another sits in a curved skiff and works the oars where he had lately been ploughing;
sentences.n: 'hic ... alter ... ille ... hic' runs on through the next line as 'one man ... another ... that one ... this one': a catalogue of the world turned upside down. The edition prints 'ararat' — syncopated 'araverat', 'he had ploughed'; some editions print 'arabat', 'he was ploughing', which leaves the ploughman still at work when the water takes him.

sentences.t:
ille supra segetes aut mersae culmina villae
navigat, hic summa piscem deprendit in ulmo.
sentences.l:
that one sails above the crops or the roof-peaks
of a drowned farmhouse; this one takes a fish in the top of an elm.
sentences.i: One sails over the standing corn, or over the roof-peaks of a sunken farmhouse; another catches a fish in the crown of an elm.
sentences.n: 'summa in ulmo' — 'summus' used predicatively means not 'the highest elm' but 'the top of the elm'; the same idiom lies behind 'in medio ponto', 'in mid-sea'. The fish in the treetop is an adynaton, the figure of the impossible thing, and these lines are built out of them.

sentences.t:
Figitur in viridi, si fors tulit, ancora prato,
aut subiecta terunt curvae vineta carinae;
sentences.l:
An anchor is fixed in a green meadow, if chance has so brought it,
or curved keels graze the vineyards lying beneath them;
sentences.n: 'si fors tulit' is a parenthesis meaning roughly 'as it may happen'; the perfect is gnomic, stating what happens in general rather than once. 'subiecta' means thrown underneath — the vines are the sea-floor now.

sentences.t:
et, modo qua graciles gramen carpsere capellae,
nunc ibi deformes ponunt sua corpora phocae.
sentences.l:
and where slender she-goats lately cropped the grass,
now there misshapen seals lay down their bodies.
sentences.n: 'carpsere' = 'carpserunt', the '-ere' perfect again. 'modo ... nunc' sets the two pictures in the same place, which is the engine of the whole passage; and the goat and the seal are chosen for how badly they match.

sentences.t:
Mirantur sub aqua lucos urbesque domosque
Nereides, silvasque tenent delphines et altis
incursant ramis agitataque robora pulsant.
sentences.l:
They marvel beneath the water at groves and cities and houses —
the Nereids; and dolphins hold the woods and against the high
branches they charge, and strike the shaken oaks.
sentences.i: The Nereids marvel at groves and cities and houses down under the water; dolphins take possession of the woods, charge the high branches, and knock against the tossing oaks.
sentences.n: The subject 'Nereides' is held back to the start of the next line — we see the wondering before we learn who is doing it. The Nereids are the fifty sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus. 'incurro' takes the dative of what is run against, hence 'altis ... ramis'.

sentences.t:
Nat lupus inter oves, fulvos vehit unda leones,
unda vehit tigres, nec vires fulminis apro,
crura nec ablato prosunt velocia cervo.
sentences.l:
The wolf swims among sheep; the wave carries tawny lions,
the wave carries tigers; nor does the strength of the thunderbolt avail the boar,
nor his swift legs the stag, once he is swept away.
sentences.i: The wolf swims among the sheep; the flood carries tawny lions, the flood carries tigers; the boar's lightning force is no use to him now, nor his swift legs to the stag once the water has him.
sentences.n: 'vires fulminis' — the boar's tusk-stroke was proverbially a thunderbolt, so this is his own lightning-strength, not Jupiter's weapon. 'apro' and 'cervo' are datives with 'prosunt', 'are of use to'; 'ablato' agrees with 'cervo', 'to the stag once carried off'.

sentences.t:
Quaesitisque diu terris, ubi sistere possit,
in mare lassatis volucris vaga decidit alis.
sentences.l:
And with lands long sought for, where it might come to rest,
the wandering bird falls into the sea on wearied wings.
sentences.i: And after long searching for land where it might settle, the wandering bird drops into the sea on worn-out wings.
sentences.n: 'quaesitis terris' is an ablative absolute again — 'with lands sought'; 'lassatis alis' beside it is a plain ablative of means. 'ubi sistere possit' is a relative clause of purpose, hence the subjunctive: land *on which it could* settle.

sentences.t:
Obruerat tumulos inmensa licentia ponti,
pulsabantque novi montana cacumina fluctus.
sentences.l:
The measureless licence of the sea had buried the hills,
and new waves were beating on the mountain summits.
sentences.i: The sea's unmeasured licence had buried the hills, and waves never seen before beat on the mountain tops.
sentences.n: 'licentia' is licence in the strict sense — a freedom taken without leave; the sea has slipped its bounds the way a lawless man does. 'novi ... fluctus' are new because no wave was ever there before.

sentences.t:
Maxima pars unda rapitur; quibus unda pepercit,
illos longa domant inopi ieiunia victu.
sentences.l:
The greatest part is snatched away by the wave; those whom the wave spared,
long fastings with scant food subdue them.
sentences.i: The greater part is carried off by the water; those the water spared are broken by long starvation on what little food there is.
sentences.n: 'parco' takes the dative, so the relative is 'quibus' and not an accusative; the main clause then picks the whole thing up again with 'illos' as object of 'domant'. That resumptive pronoun is ordinary Latin whenever the relative clause runs out ahead of its main clause.

sentences.t:
Separat Aonios Oetaeis Phocis ab arvis,
terra ferax, dum terra fuit, sed tempore in illo
pars maris et latus subitarum campus aquarum.
sentences.l:
Phocis separates the Aonian fields from the Oetaean,
a fertile land, while it was land — but at that time
a part of the sea, and a broad plain of sudden waters.
sentences.i: Phocis divides the fields of Aonia from those of Oeta: a fertile land, while it was land — but at that time part of the sea, a wide plain of water risen in a moment.
sentences.n: Aonia is Boeotia, Oeta the mountain on the Thessalian border; Phocis lies between them, and holds Parnassus and Delphi. 'Aonios' is masculine and cannot agree with neuter 'arvis' — supply a masculine noun with it, the Aonian fields set against the Oetaean. 'dum terra fuit', three words, is the whole flood. The last line has no verb at all: after 'sed' the reader supplies 'it was'.

sentences.t:
Mons ibi verticibus petit arduus astra duobus,
nomine Parnasus, superantque cacumina nubes.
sentences.l:
There a steep mountain reaches for the stars with two summits,
Parnassus by name, and its peaks pass beyond the clouds.
sentences.i: There a steep mountain reaches up to the stars with twin summits — Parnassus by name — and its peaks stand higher than the clouds.
sentences.n: 'verticibus ... duobus' is an ablative of means split wide around the verb and its object, so that the two peaks frame the line as they frame the mountain. Parnassus rises above Delphi, and its twin heads were a stock feature of it in verse.

sentences.t:
Hic ubi Deucalion (nam cetera texerat aequor)
cum consorte tori parva rate vectus adhaesit,
sentences.l:
Here, when Deucalion (for the sea had covered all else),
carried in a small raft with the partner of his bed, came to rest,
sentences.i: Here, when Deucalion — the sea had covered everything else — came to rest, carried in a small raft with the partner of his bed,
sentences.n: Deucalion is the son of Prometheus; 'consors tori', 'sharer of the bed', is Pyrrha, who is not named for another thirty lines. 'adhaesit' is what a boat does when it grounds and sticks. The parenthesis explains why a mountain-top is where he lands.

sentences.t:
Corycidas nymphas et numina montis adorant
fatidicamque Themin, quae tunc oracla tenebat.
sentences.l:
they worship the Corycian nymphs and the mountain's divinities
and prophetic Themis, who then held the oracles.
sentences.i: the two of them worship the Corycian nymphs and the powers of the mountain and prophetic Themis, who held the oracle in those days.
sentences.n: The verb 'adorant' is plural though only Deucalion has been named as subject — Pyrrha is inside 'cum consorte tori' and the verb quietly takes her in. The Corycian cave is on Parnassus. 'oracla' is syncopated 'oracula'. Themis, a Titaness and the power of settled right, held Delphi before Apollo did.

sentences.t:
Non illo melior quisquam nec amantior aequi
vir fuit aut illa metuentior ulla deorum.
sentences.l:
No man was better than he, nor more loving of the right,
nor any woman more fearing of the gods than she.
sentences.i: No man was better than he, or more in love with what was right; no woman more in awe of the gods than she.
sentences.n: 'illo' and 'illa' are ablatives of comparison — 'than he', 'than she' — and Ovid sets the pair at the two ends of the sentence. 'amantior aequi' and 'metuentior deorum' are comparatives of present participles used as adjectives, each with a genitive of the thing loved or feared.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter ut liquidis stagnare paludibus orbem
et superesse virum de tot modo milibus unum,
et superesse videt de tot modo milibus unam,
innocuos ambo, cultores numinis ambo,
sentences.l:
When Jupiter sees that the world lies stagnant in clear marshes,
and that out of so many thousands but now one man survives,
and sees that out of so many thousands but now one woman survives,
both harmless, both worshippers of the divine,
sentences.i: When Jupiter sees the world lying stagnant in clear marsh-water, and one man left out of so many thousands a moment ago, and one woman left out of so many thousands a moment ago, both of them harmless, both of them worshippers of heaven,
sentences.n: 'ut ... videt' is 'when he sees', with the verb held back to the third line; everything before it is indirect statement carried by 'stagnare' and 'superesse'. Lines 325 and 326 are the same line twice over but for 'virum ... unum' against 'videt ... unam' — Ovid gets two survivors out of one construction, and the repetition is the point.

sentences.t:
nubila disiecit nimbisque aquilone remotis
et caelo terras ostendit et aethera terris.
sentences.l:
he scattered the clouds, and with the rain-clouds driven off by the north wind
he showed both the lands to the sky and the upper air to the lands.
sentences.i: he broke up the clouds and, the rain driven away by the north wind, showed the lands to the sky and the sky to the lands.
sentences.n: 'nimbis aquilone remotis' is another ablative absolute, and Aquilo is out of his cave again now the work is done. Line 329 is a chiasmus — 'caelo terras ... aethera terris', sky-lands-air-lands — the two halves of the world handed back to each other.

sentences.t:
Nec maris ira manet, positoque tricuspide telo
mulcet aquas rector pelagi
sentences.l:
Nor does the sea's anger remain; and with his three-pointed weapon laid down
the ruler of the deep gentles the waters
sentences.i: The sea's anger does not last either: the ruler of the deep lays his three-pointed weapon aside and calms the water
sentences.n: 'posito ... telo' is one more ablative absolute; 'tricuspide', three-pointed, is the trident named by its shape. Neptune is again given by his office rather than his name. 'mulcet' is the verb for soothing an animal or a child.

sentences.t:
supraque profundum
exstantem atque umeros innato murice tectum
caeruleum Tritona vocat
sentences.l:
and — standing out above the deep,
and covered as to his shoulders with shell grown into him —
sea-blue Triton he calls,
sentences.i: and calls sea-blue Triton, who stands up out of the deep, his shoulders crusted with shells grown fast into him,
sentences.n: 'umeros ... tectum' — the Greek accusative of respect once more, covered *as to* his shoulders. 'murex' is the spiny shell that gave the ancient purple dye, and 'innato' says the shells have grown onto him and are part of his body. Triton is Neptune's son and his herald.

sentences.t:
conchaeque sonanti
inspirare iubet fluctusque et flumina signo
iam revocare dato.
sentences.l:
and bids him blow into the sounding conch,
and call back the floods and the rivers, the signal
now having been given.
sentences.i: and bids him breathe into the echoing conch and call the floods and rivers back, now that the signal is given.
sentences.n: 'signo ... dato' is an ablative absolute split across the line-end — 'signo' closes 334 and 'dato' opens 335, with 'iam revocare' pushed in between. 'conchae ... inspirare' takes the dative: to breathe *into* it.

sentences.t:
Cava bucina sumitur illi,
tortilis, in latum quae turbine crescit ab imo,
sentences.l:
The hollow trumpet is taken up by him,
a spiralling thing, which widens out from its lowest whorl,
sentences.i: He takes up the hollow horn — a spiral, widening out from the small end of its coil —
sentences.n: 'illi' is a dative of agent with the passive 'sumitur', 'taken up by him' — a construction Latin normally keeps for gerundives and the poets use freely. 'turbine' is the tapering twist of the shell, 'in latum' the flare at the mouth.

sentences.t:
bucina, quae medio concepit ubi aera ponto,
litora voce replet sub utroque iacentia Phoebo.
sentences.l:
the trumpet which, when it has drawn in the air in mid-sea,
fills with its voice the shores that lie under either Phoebus.
sentences.i: the horn which, once it has taken in air out in mid-ocean, fills with its voice the shores lying under sunrise and sunset alike.
sentences.n: 'sub utroque ... Phoebo' — under both suns, that is, under the rising and the setting sun: the shores of the whole world. 'ubi' is postponed inside its own clause, a licence verse takes freely; read it as 'ubi medio ponto aera concepit'. Picking 'bucina' up again at the head of 337, after the whole description of the shell, restarts the sentence from the word it had left.

sentences.t:
Tunc quoque, ut ora dei madida rorantia barba
contigit et cecinit iussos inflata receptus,
sentences.l:
Then too, when it touched the god's lips, dripping with his wet beard,
and, blown, sounded the ordered retreat,
sentences.i: Then too, once it had touched the god's lips, wet with his dripping beard, and, filled with breath, sounded the retreat that had been ordered,
sentences.n: The subject of 'contigit' and 'cecinit' is still the horn, not the god. 'receptus' is accusative plural of a military word — the trumpet-call that brings troops back, so that the flood is still an army under orders. 'quoque' is once more the plain adverb 'too'.

sentences.t:
omnibus audita est telluris et aequoris undis,
et quibus est undis audita, coercuit omnes.
sentences.l:
it was heard by all the waters of land and sea,
and by what waters it was heard, it held them all in check.
sentences.i: it was heard by every water of land and sea; and all the waters it was heard by, it checked.
sentences.n: 'quibus est undis audita' has the antecedent 'undis' pulled inside the relative clause, and the main clause then takes the whole of it up with 'omnes'. English has to unpick it: 'the waters by which it was heard — all of them it restrained'.

sentences.t:
Iam mare litus habet, plenos capit alveus amnes,
flumina subsidunt collesque exire videntur,
surgit humus, crescunt loca decrescentibus undis,
sentences.l:
Now the sea has a shore, the channel holds its brimming rivers,
the streams sink down and the hills are seen to come out,
the ground rises, places grow as the waters shrink,
sentences.i: Now the sea has a shore again, the river-bed holds its full streams, the rivers drop, the hills are seen coming up, the ground rises, the land grows as the water goes down,
sentences.n: 'decrescentibus undis' is one more ablative absolute, and it is set against 'crescunt' in the same line: the land grows by exactly what the water loses. Six clauses in three lines, all present tense and all short — that is the pace of the recovery.

sentences.t:
postque diem longam nudata cacumina silvae
ostendunt limumque tenent in fronde relictum.
sentences.l:
and after a long time the woods show their bared crowns
and hold the mud left behind on their leaves.
sentences.i: and after a long while the woods show their tops bare again, with the silt still lying in the foliage.
sentences.n: 'diem longam' — 'dies' is masculine of a day of the calendar but feminine when it means a stretch of time, which is why 'longam' is feminine here and why the phrase is 'after a long while' rather than 'after a long day'. The mud in the leaves is the one detail that measures the flood: the water stood above the treetops.

sentences.t:
Redditus orbis erat. Quem postquam vidit inanem
et desolatas agere alta silentia terras,
Deucalion lacrimis ita Pyrrham adfatur obortis:
sentences.l:
The world had been given back. And when he saw it empty,
and the deserted lands keeping deep silences,
Deucalion, with tears risen, thus addresses Pyrrha:
sentences.i: The world had been given back. And when he saw it empty, and the deserted lands keeping a deep silence, Deucalion's tears rose and he spoke to Pyrrha:
sentences.n: 'Quem' at the head of the sentence is a connecting relative — 'and it', not 'which'; Latin joins sentences this way where English begins a new one. 'agere alta silentia' carries the indirect statement on after 'vidit'. 'lacrimis ... obortis' is an ablative absolute wrapped around the whole line.

sentences.t:
“O soror, o coniunx, o femina sola superstes,
quam commune mihi genus et patruelis origo,
deinde torus iunxit, nunc ipsa pericula iungunt,
sentences.l:
'O sister, O wife, O woman sole surviving,
whom a common stock and a cousin's descent,
then the marriage-bed joined to me — now the perils themselves join us —
sentences.i: 'O sister, O wife, O only woman left alive — whom a common stock and a cousin's blood, and then our marriage, joined to me, and whom now the dangers themselves join —
sentences.n: Three vocatives in a rising line. 'soror' is not loose affection but kinship: Deucalion's father Prometheus and Pyrrha's father Epimetheus were brothers, so 'patruelis origo' means they are first cousins on the father's side. The tenses climb with the relation — perfect 'iunxit' for what joined them once, present 'iungunt' for what joins them now.

sentences.t:
terrarum, quascumque vident occasus et ortus,
nos duo turba sumus; possedit cetera pontus.
sentences.l:
of the lands, all of them that sunset and sunrise look upon,
we two are the crowd; the sea has taken the rest.
sentences.i: of all the lands that sunrise and sunset look upon, we two are the population; the sea has taken everything else.
sentences.n: 'terrarum' is a partitive genitive hanging on 'turba': the crowd *of* all those lands is two people. 'occasus et ortus', setting and rising, is the ordinary way of saying west and east and so 'everywhere'. The sentence is built as a paradox and turns on the single word 'turba'.

sentences.t:
Haec quoque adhuc vitae non est fiducia nostrae
certa satis; terrent etiam nunc nubila mentem.
sentences.l:
This confidence of ours in living is not yet
sure enough either; even now the clouds terrify my mind.
sentences.i: Nor is even this confidence in our own survival sure enough yet: the clouds frighten me still.
sentences.n: 'fiducia vitae nostrae' is an objective genitive — confidence *in* our life, not confidence belonging to it. 'certa satis' is held over to the next line, so the doubt lands after the noun it undoes. 'quoque' is the adverb again.

sentences.t:
Quis tibi, si sine me fatis erepta fuisses,
nunc animus, miseranda, foret? quo sola timorem
ferre modo posses? quo consolante doleres?
sentences.l:
What heart would be yours now, poor woman, if without me
you had been snatched from the fates? in what way could you bear
your fear alone? with whom to console you would you grieve?
sentences.i: What spirit would you have now, poor soul, if you had been saved from death and I not with you? How could you bear the fear alone? Who would there be to comfort your grief?
sentences.n: A mixed unreal condition — pluperfect 'fuisses' in the protasis, imperfect 'foret' (= 'esset') with 'nunc' for a present result that did not come about. 'fatis erepta' is rescued FROM the fates: he is imagining her surviving without him, not dying. 'miseranda' is a gerundive used as a vocative, 'you who must be pitied'. 'quo ... modo' is split around 'sola timorem / ferre', and 'quo consolante' is an ablative absolute, 'with whom consoling'.

sentences.t:
Namque ego (crede mihi) si te quoque pontus haberet,
te sequerer, coniunx, et me quoque pontus haberet.
O utinam possim populos reparare paternis
artibus atque animas formatae infundere terrae!
sentences.l:
For I — believe me — if the sea held you too,
would follow you, wife, and the sea would hold me too.
O that I might have power to remake the peoples by my father's
arts, and pour souls into moulded earth!
sentences.i: For I — believe me — if the sea had you, would follow you, wife, and the sea would have me too. Oh, if only I could make the peoples over again by my father's arts, and pour souls into shaped clay!
sentences.n: 'haberet ... sequerer ... haberet' is an unreal present condition, imperfect subjunctive throughout, and the same verb closes both lines so that his fate is hers word for word. 'paternis artibus' — Prometheus, Deucalion's father, made the first men out of clay, so the wish is for precisely the thing his father could do and he cannot. 'utinam possim' is a wish with the present subjunctive, still open rather than shut off.

sentences.t:
Nunc genus in nobis restat mortale duobus
(sic visum superis) hominumque exempla manemus.”
sentences.l:
Now the mortal race is left in us two
(so it seemed good to those above), and we remain the specimens of men.'
sentences.i: As it is, the mortal race is left in the two of us — so the gods above have decided — and we remain as the only sample of mankind.'
sentences.n: 'sic visum superis' is impersonal 'visum est' with the dative, 'so it seemed good to those above'; dropping 'est' makes it curt, like a verdict handed down. 'exempla' are samples — the pieces kept to show what the whole was like. They are the surviving copies of the human kind.

sentences.t:
Dixerat, et flebant. Placuit caeleste precari
numen et auxilium per sacras quaerere sortes.
sentences.l:
He had spoken, and they were weeping. It seemed good to pray to the heavenly
power, and to seek help through the sacred lots.
sentences.i: He had spoken, and they wept. They resolved to pray to the powers of heaven and to seek help through the sacred oracle.
sentences.n: Three tenses in one line — pluperfect 'Dixerat' to shut the speech, imperfect 'flebant' for weeping that goes on, perfect 'Placuit' for the decision that ends it. 'placuit' is impersonal, 'it was resolved', with the infinitives as its subject. 'sortes' are the lots by which an oracle answers, and so the answer itself.

sentences.t:
Nulla mora est: adeunt pariter Cephisidas undas,
ut nondum liquidas, sic iam vada nota secantes.
sentences.l:
There is no delay: side by side they approach the waters of Cephisus,
not yet clear, but already cutting their known channels.
sentences.i: No delay: together they go to the waters of Cephisus — not clear yet, but already cutting their old familiar bed.
sentences.n: 'ut nondum liquidas, sic iam ... secantes' — 'ut ... sic' is concessive here, 'though ... yet'. The Cephisus rises at the foot of Parnassus and runs east through the plain of Phocis. The detail is exact: a river just after a flood is still thick with silt but back between its banks.

sentences.t:
Inde ubi libatos inroravere liquores
vestibus et capiti, flectunt vestigia sanctae
ad delubra deae, quorum fastigia turpi
pallebant musco stabantque sine ignibus arae.
sentences.l:
Then, when they had sprinkled the water they had drawn
on their garments and their heads, they turn their steps to the shrine
of the holy goddess, whose gables were pale with foul
moss, and whose altars stood without fires.
sentences.i: Then, when they had sprinkled the drawn water over their clothes and their heads, they turn their steps towards the shrine of the holy goddess — its gables pale with ugly moss, its altars standing without fire.
sentences.n: 'inroravere' = 'inroraverunt', the '-ere' perfect again. 'sanctae ... deae' is split wide around 'ad delubra', so the shrine arrives before the goddess it belongs to; 'quorum' agrees with 'delubra', not with 'deae'. Moss on the pediment and no fire on the altar say the same thing twice over: nobody has come here in a long time.

sentences.t:
Ut templi tetigere gradus, procumbit uterque
pronus humi gelidoque pavens dedit oscula saxo
sentences.l:
When they touched the temple's steps, each of them falls forward
face down on the ground, and, trembling, gave kisses to the cold stone.
sentences.i: When they touched the temple steps, both of them go down face to the ground and, trembling, kissed the cold stone.
sentences.n: 'tetigere' = 'tetigerunt'. Present 'procumbit' and perfect 'dedit' stand side by side in one sentence: the falling happens before our eyes, the kiss is already given. 'humi' is a locative, 'on the ground'.

sentences.t:
atque ita “si precibus” dixerunt “numina iustis
victa remollescunt, si flectitur ira deorum,
sentences.l:
and thus 'if by just prayers,' they said, 'divine powers
are overcome and soften, if the anger of the gods is bent,
sentences.i: and this is what they said: 'If divine powers are overcome by just prayers and relent, if the anger of the gods can be bent,
sentences.n: 'dixerunt' is dropped inside the quotation instead of before it, a mannerism Ovid likes: the speech starts, and only then are we told who is speaking. 'precibus iustis' is ablative with 'victa'; 'remollescunt' is an inceptive verb, to *begin* to soften again.

sentences.t:
dic, Themi, qua generis damnum reparabile nostri
arte sit, et mersis fer opem, mitissima, rebus.”
sentences.l:
tell, Themis, by what art the loss of our race
is repairable, and bring aid, most gentle one, to a drowned world.'
sentences.i: tell us, Themis, by what art the loss of our race can be made good, and bring help, gentlest of powers, to a world gone under.'
sentences.n: 'qua ... arte' is split across the line-end with the whole of 'generis damnum reparabile nostri' between the two words, so the question hangs open until 'arte sit'. 'sit' is subjunctive because it is an indirect question. 'mersis ... rebus' is dative with 'fer opem' — bring help to things that have gone under.

sentences.t: Mota dea est sortemque dedit:
sentences.l: The goddess was moved, and gave her response:
sentences.n: 'Mota' is moved in the sense of stirred to act — the very thing they had asked for in 'si flectitur ira deorum'. 'sortem' is the oracle's answer, and what follows is it.

sentences.t:
“Discedite templo
et velate caput cinctasque resolvite vestes
ossaque post tergum magnae iactate parentis.”
sentences.l:
'Depart from the temple,
and veil your heads and loosen your girded robes,
and throw behind your backs the bones of the great mother.'
sentences.n: 'templo' is a bare ablative of separation without a preposition, which is normal with 'discedo' in verse. Veiling the head is standard Roman ritual practice, and loosening a knotted or girded garment belongs to rites too, so the orders sound proper until the last of them. 'magnae ... parentis' is the riddle of this story, and Ovid keeps the two words apart to the end of the line with the imperative 'iactate' driven between them.

sentences.t:
Obstipuere diu, rumpitque silentia voce
Pyrrha prior iussisque deae parere recusat,
sentences.l:
Long they stood stunned; and Pyrrha first breaks the silence with her voice
and refuses to obey the commands of the goddess,
sentences.n: 'Obstipuere' = 'obstipuerunt'. Perfect and then present within one line: the long silence is over and done, the breaking of it happens now. 'iussis parere' — 'pareo' takes the dative of the thing obeyed.

sentences.t:
detque sibi veniam pavido rogat ore, pavetque
laedere iactatis maternas ossibus umbras.
sentences.l:
and with frightened lips asks that pardon be given her, and dreads
to injure her mother's shade with thrown bones.
sentences.i: and asks in a frightened voice to be forgiven, in dread of doing violence to her mother's ghost with bones thrown about.
sentences.n: 'detque ... rogat' is 'rogat' with a bare subjunctive and no 'ut' — verse drops the conjunction freely. 'iactatis ... ossibus' is ablative, and 'maternas ... umbras' shows how she has read the oracle: the great mother is her own mother, and the bones are her mother's bones.

sentences.t:
Interea repetunt caecis obscura latebris
verba datae sortis secum inter seque volutant.
sentences.l:
Meanwhile they go over again the words, dark with blind hiding-places,
of the response given, and turn them over within themselves and between themselves.
sentences.i: Meanwhile they go over the words of the oracle again — dark with blind hiding-places — turning them over each in his own mind and between the two of them.
sentences.n: 'caecis ... latebris' is an ablative of respect with 'obscura': the words are dark by reason of the coverts in them. 'secum inter seque' sets private thought against shared talk in three words, tied by the double '-que'. And 'obscura ... verba' is itself split across the line-end, which is exactly what the phrase describes.

sentences.t:
Inde Promethides placidis Epimethida dictis
mulcet et “aut fallax” ait “est sollertia nobis,
aut pia sunt nullumque nefas oracula suadent.
sentences.l:
Then the son of Prometheus soothes the daughter of Epimetheus
with calming words, and 'either,' he says, 'false is the shrewdness we have,
or the oracles are holy and urge no wrong.
sentences.i: Then the son of Prometheus quiets the daughter of Epimetheus with soothing words: 'Either our own cleverness is playing us false,' he says, 'or the oracles are holy and urge nothing wicked.
sentences.n: 'Promethides' and 'Epimethida' are Greek patronymics, and 'Epimethida' keeps the Greek accusative in '-a'. The names mean 'Forethought' and 'Afterthought', and it is Forethought's son who works the riddle out. 'nobis' is a dative of possession — 'the shrewdness we have' — with the predicate 'fallax' thrown to the front. 'sollertia' is practical cleverness.

sentences.t:
Magna parens terra est, lapides in corpore terrae
ossa reor dici; iacere hos post terga iubemur.”
sentences.l:
The great parent is the earth; the stones in the earth's body
I think are called her bones; we are bidden to throw these behind our backs.'
sentences.i: The great parent is the earth; the stones in the earth's body are what I take to be called her bones — and it is these we are told to throw behind us.'
sentences.n: 'ossa reor dici' is indirect statement: 'lapides' is subject accusative of 'dici' and 'ossa' the predicate accusative, 'that the stones are called bones'. 'iubemur' with an infinitive is the personal passive of 'iubeo', which Latin prefers to an impersonal turn. The whole reading hangs on taking 'parens' of the earth rather than of a mother — the ordinary Roman usage he has simply remembered.

sentences.t:
Coniugis augurio quamquam Titania mota est,
spes tamen in dubio est: adeo caelestibus ambo
diffidunt monitis. Sed quid temptare nocebit?
sentences.l:
Although the Titan's daughter was moved by her husband's reading of it,
still hope stands in doubt: so far do the two of them
distrust the warnings of heaven. But what harm will trying do?
sentences.i: Though the Titan's daughter was moved by her husband's reading, hope still hangs in the balance: so deeply do they both mistrust the warnings of heaven. Still — what harm in trying?
sentences.n: 'Titania' is Pyrrha, granddaughter of the Titan Iapetus through Epimetheus. 'diffidunt' takes the dative, 'monitis', and 'in dubio est' is a fixed phrase, 'is in the balance'. The closing question is theirs, not the narrator's: Ovid slides into their thought without marking it.

sentences.t:
Discedunt velantque caput tunicasque recingunt
et iussos lapides sua post vestigia mittunt.
sentences.l:
They depart and veil their heads and ungird their tunics
and throw the stones they were ordered to throw behind their footsteps.
sentences.i: They leave, veil their heads, loosen their tunics, and throw the stones as ordered behind their steps.
sentences.n: 'iussos lapides' — the stones were not ordered; the throwing was. Latin lets the participle slide onto the object like this and English has to unpick it. The edition prints 'Discedunt', which answers Themis's own 'Discedite'; some editions print 'descendunt', 'they go down' — the temple steps rather than the temple.

sentences.t:
Saxa (quis hoc credat, nisi sit pro teste vetustas?)
ponere duritiem coepere suumque rigorem
mollirique mora mollitaque ducere formam.
sentences.l:
The stones (who would believe this, were antiquity not there for witness?)
began to put off their hardness and their stiffness,
and to be softened by lapse of time, and, softened, to take on shape.
sentences.i: The stones — who would believe it, if antiquity were not there to vouch for it? — began to lose their hardness and their stiffness, to grow soft as time passed, and, once soft, to take on a shape.
sentences.n: 'quis hoc credat' is a potential subjunctive, 'who would believe', matched by 'nisi sit'; the aside is Ovid's own, and sheer age is offered as the only witness there can be. 'coepere' = 'coeperunt'. 'mollirique' is passive among active infinitives, and 'mollita' takes the same verb up again at once: the stones are softened, and then act for themselves.

sentences.t:
Mox ubi creverunt naturaque mitior illis
contigit, ut quaedam, sic non manifesta, videri
forma potest hominis,
sentences.l:
Soon, when they had grown, and a gentler nature had come
to them, there can be seen — of a sort, yet not clearly —
the shape of a human being,
sentences.i: Soon, once they had grown and a gentler nature had come to them, a human shape could be made out — of a sort, but not distinctly —
sentences.n: 'ut quaedam, sic non manifesta' balances its two halves: a shape of some sort, yet not a distinct one. 'contigit' with the dative is what falls to someone's lot. 'forma ... hominis' is held to the very end, after the whole hedging parenthesis.

sentences.t:
sed, uti de marmore coepta,
non exacta satis rudibusque simillima signis.
sentences.l:
but, like things begun out of marble,
not finished enough, and very like statues still in the rough.
sentences.i: but like work begun in marble and left unfinished — very like statues not yet worked up.
sentences.n: 'coepta' is neuter plural agreeing with an understood 'signa', which 'signis' then supplies at the end of the next line. 'simillima' is the superlative of 'similis' and takes the dative. The comparison is a sculptor's, and Ovid keeps to the workshop for the whole of this change.

sentences.t:
Quae tamen ex illis aliquo pars umida suco
et terrena fuit, versa est in corporis usum;
sentences.l:
Yet what part of them was moist with some sap
and earthy, was turned to the use of a body;
sentences.i: But whatever part of them held some moisture and was of earth was turned to serve as flesh;
sentences.n: 'Quae ... pars' has the antecedent inside the relative clause again — 'what part ... that part'. 'aliquo ... suco' is an ablative of respect with 'umida'. From here to the end the lines work through the body piece by piece, matching each part to what the stone was.

sentences.t:
quod solidum est flectique nequit, mutatur in ossa;
quae modo vena fuit, sub eodem nomine mansit;
sentences.l:
what is solid and cannot be bent is changed into bones;
what was lately a vein has remained under the same name;
sentences.n: 'vena' is a vein of rock in a stone and a vein in a body, and it is one and the same word for both — so this metamorphosis leaves exactly one thing untouched, the word. 'sub eodem nomine mansit' says so outright, and the couplet exists for that point.

sentences.t:
inque brevi spatio superorum numine saxa
missa viri manibus faciem traxere virorum,
et de femineo reparata est femina iactu.
sentences.l:
and in a short space, by the will of the gods above, the stones
thrown by the man's hands took on the face of men,
and from the woman's throw a woman was restored.
sentences.i: and in a short while, by the will of the gods above, the stones thrown from the man's hands took on the faces of men, and from the woman's throw a woman was made again.
sentences.n: 'traxere' = 'traxerunt'. The two lines are built on the play 'viri ... virorum' and 'femineo ... femina': the thrower's sex decides the stone's, and the word-endings carry the whole explanation. 'superorum numine' is an ablative of means — the change is the gods' doing, not the stones'.

sentences.t:
Inde genus durum sumus experiensque laborum
et documenta damus qua simus origine nati.
sentences.l:
From that we are a hard race, and one that endures hardships,
and we give proof of the stock from which we were born.
sentences.n: 'experiens laborum' is a present participle used as an adjective with a genitive — having experience of, standing up to, hardships. 'qua simus origine nati' is an indirect question, hence the subjunctive 'simus', with 'origine' as ablative of source. The whole story has been told to account for one word: we are 'durum' because we came out of stone.
